warmup.q: A payment record's amount is "12x50", so parsing it fails every time. Your at-least-once consumer from lesson 7 lets the exception escape, and Kubernetes restarts the pod. What happens to the payments behind it in the same partition?
options: They are processed: Kafka skips a record that fails three times
They wait indefinitely: every restart starts at the committed offset, reaches the same record and crashes again
Kafka moves the bad record to a dead-letter topic after max.poll.interval.ms
warmup.why: Kafka has no idea your code failed; the plain consumer has no retry limit and no dead-letter topic. The committed offset stays before the bad record, so every restart replays from there and fails at the same place. Dead-letter topics exist only if your code or framework writes them. The first option is the tempting belief that Kafka gives up on a record for you. A queue broker would at least count the attempts: a RabbitMQ quorum queue gives up on a message after 20 deliveries by default and drops it, or dead-letters it if you set a dead-letter exchange. A Kafka consumer group counts nothing.

sections.h: One record that always fails stops its whole partition
sections.html:
Lesson 1 of this track met the poison message in a queue: a message that crashes every consumer that takes it, is redelivered, and crashes the next one. On a log the same record does more damage. This lesson shows why, and builds what the log leaves you to build yourself.

pay-3 arrives with the amount 12x50. Somebody's payment form let a letter through. Parsing it throws NumberFormatException, and it will throw every time.

Run that through the at-least-once loop from lesson 7. The loop processes the batch, and the exception escapes before the commit. The pod restarts, starts at the group's committed offset, processes pay-0 to pay-2 again, reaches pay-3 and crashes again. It will do this forever. The Try-it below shows three rounds of it.

A partition is a log with one bookmark per group, and the bookmark can only move past a record once the consumer is done with it. So one record that can't be done holds back everything behind it in its partition. If that partition receives 30 payments a second, 108,000 pile up behind pay-3 in an hour. The other partitions keep flowing, which makes it easy to miss: the group's total lag barely moves. A record that fails every time you process it is a poison pill.

Compare lesson 1's queue. Its broker keeps a state for every message, so while a bad message is redelivered, the messages behind it go to other consumers. And the broker counts the attempts: since RabbitMQ 4.0, a quorum queue stops after 20 deliveries by default and drops the message, or dead-letters it if a dead-letter exchange is set. A Kafka consumer group keeps one bookmark per partition and counts nothing, so nothing gives up and nothing behind the record gets past. That is head-of-line blocking, the price of the log's per-partition order. Everything the queue broker did for its poison message, a Kafka consumer has to do itself.

It can fail in two places. In your own code, as here: a bad amount, an unknown currency, a NullPointerException in a mapper. Or inside poll, in the deserializer, when the bytes aren't what the deserializer expects: a producer that switched to Avro, a corrupted record. Then poll hands out the good records in front of the bad one, and on the next call throws RecordDeserializationException. The exception names the partition and the offset, and in Kafka 4.4 it also carries the record's raw key and value bytes. The consumer's position stays on the bad record, so every later poll throws again. The only way past it is seek(partition, offset + 1), and if you seek without saving those bytes somewhere first, the record is gone for good.

Before choosing a fix, ask why it failed, because the answer decides what helps.

A transient failure means the record is fine and something around it was briefly wrong: the card issuer timed out, a database lock wait expired, a downstream service answered 503. The same call can succeed a second later, so retrying is right.

A permanent failure means the record, or your code, is wrong: 12x50, a currency your ledger doesn't know, a bug. Retrying gives the same exception every time, so it only wastes time and blocks the partition.

The consumer has to tell them apart, and it can only do that by the exception's type. Make that list explicit: retry the exceptions you know are transient, and treat everything else as permanent.

try.title: Watch a poison pill stop a partition
steps: From the labs folder, start the broker: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait.

Run PoisonPillDemo (command below). It writes six amounts to a new topic; the third is 12x50. Then it tries three times to get through them, each time with a fresh consumer that starts at the committed offset, as a restarted pod would. Here the handler parses the amount.
Predict, then run it again with -Pargs=deserialize: now the value deserializer parses the amount, inside poll. On the third try it seeks past the bad record.

position stays " + c.position(tp)); if (attempt < 3) break; // crash: the next try starts at the committed offset c.seek(tp, e.offset() + 1); // the only way past it: skip the record c.commitSync(Map.of(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(e.offset() + 1))); System.out.println("try " + attempt + ": seek to " + (e.offset() + 1) + ": offset " + e.offset() + " is skipped, and nobody will see it again"); } } } } else { try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<>(config, new StringDeserializer(), new StringDeserializer())) { c.assign(List.of(tp)); try { while (c.position(tp) < 6) { ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = c.poll(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) { long cents = Long.parseLong(r.value()); // the handler: throws NumberFormatException on 12x50 System.out.println("try " + attempt + ": offset " + r.offset() + " applied " + cents + " cents"); } if (!records.isEmpty()) c.commitSync(Map.of(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(c.position(tp)))); // after the whole batch } } catch (NumberFormatException e) { System.out.println("try " + attempt + ": crashed: " + e + "; sections.h: Retry a few times, then move the record to a dead-letter topic
sections.html:
For a transient failure, the simplest fix is to try again, in place, before moving on: call the handler, and if it throws a transient exception, wait and call it again. Two rules make this safe. Cap the attempts, at 3 for example, because an unbounded retry is the poison pill again. And make the wait grow, 100 ms, then 200 ms, then 400 ms (exponential backoff), so a struggling card issuer isn't hammered by every consumer at once. These retries run inside the poll loop, so all of them must fit inside max.poll.interval.ms from lesson 8: three tries with sub-second waits are nothing, but six tries of 30 seconds each would use 3 of its 5 minutes.

When the attempts run out, or the failure is permanent, the consumer has to get the record out of the way. Logging it and committing past it is the tempting answer, and it loses the payment: one ledger entry missing, and nobody notices until month-end reconciliation. Write it to a dead-letter topic (DLT) instead, such as payments.DLT: the same key and value, plus headers that say where it came from and why it failed.

A header is a small named value attached to a Kafka record next to its key and value: a string name and a byte array. Consumers that don't look at headers aren't affected by them. A useful dead letter carries the original topic, partition and offset, so someone can find the record and what was around it, and the exception's class and message, so they know what to fix.

The order of operations matters. Send the dead letter and wait for the broker's acknowledgement (send(...).get()), and only then commit the offset past the record:

Java
for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) {
    try {
        handleWithRetries(r);                        // transient failures: up to 3 attempts
    } catch (Exception e) {                          // permanent, or out of attempts
        dlt.send(DeadLetters.deadLetter(r, e, "payments.DLT")).get();   // acked before we move on
    }
}
consumer.commitSync(nextOffsets(records));           // only now is it safe to move the bookmark
Kotlin
for (r in records) {
    try {
        handleWithRetries(r)                         // transient failures: up to 3 attempts
    } catch (e: Exception) {                         // permanent, or out of attempts
        dlt.send(DeadLetters.deadLetter(r, e, "payments.DLT")).get()    // acked before we move on
    }
}
consumer.commitSync(nextOffsets(records))            // only now is it safe to move the bookmark

If the DLT write fails, nothing is committed, the batch comes back after a restart, and the dead letter is written then. That is lesson 7's at-least-once rule applied to failures. Here the log does better than the queue it replaced. A RabbitMQ quorum queue dead-letters by itself, but by default at-most-once: if the dead-letter target can't take the message, it's gone. At-least-once dead-lettering there needs dead-letter-strategy=at-least-once together with overflow=reject-publish. In Kafka you write the dead letter yourself, so you choose the order, and ack before commit is at-least-once.

The name is a convention. This lab uses payments.DLT. Spring for Apache Kafka 4 sends dead letters to payments-dlt by default, on the same partition number as the original. Quarkus's dead-letter-queue failure strategy writes to dead-letter-topic-<channel>. Whatever the name, a DLT needs an owner: an alert when a record lands in it, and a replay tool that sends a fixed record back to payments, where lesson 7's idempotency key keeps a replay from being applied twice.

try.title: Retry, dead-letter, carry on
steps: Run DeadLetterDemo (command below). It writes eight payments to ledger-payments. The card issuer times out twice on pay-2, and pay-3, acct-7's capture, has the amount 12x50. The consumer retries timeouts up to 3 times, sends what still fails to ledger-payments.DLT, and commits.
Predict which payments are applied, which are retried and which end up in the DLT.

Read the DLT with its headers: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic ledger-payments.DLT --partition 0 --offset earliest --formatter-property print.key=true --formatter-property print.headers=true --timeout-ms 10000.

code.title: DeadLetterDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.msg.l09.demo; import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.Admin; import org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.NewTopic; import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.ConsumerRecord; import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.KafkaConsumer; import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.OffsetAndMetadata; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer; import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord; import org.apache.kafka.common.TopicPartition; import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer; import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.*; /** * Writes eight payments to partition 0 of "ledger-payments". The card issuer times out twice on pay-2, and pay-3, * acct-7's capture, is a poison pill: its amount is "12x50". The consumer retries a timeout up to 3 times, sends a * record that still fails to "ledger-payments.DLT" with headers that say where it came from, and moves on. * Argument: "skip" (the default: acct-7's later payments are processed) or "park" (they follow the failed one to * the DLT, so no payment of acct-7 overtakes it). */ public class DeadLetterDemo { /** The card issuer did not answer in time. Worth another try. */ static class IssuerTimeout extends RuntimeException { IssuerTimeout() { super("card issuer timed out"); } } static int issuerTimeouts = 2; static void handle(ConsumerRecord<String, String> r) { String[] f = r.value().split(","); if (f[0].equals("pay-2") && issuerTimeouts-- > 0) throw new IssuerTimeout(); Long.parseLong(f[2]); // throws NumberFormatException for 12x50: bad data, never worth a retry } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean park = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("park"); String topic = "ledger-payments"; String dlt = topic + ".DLT"; TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition(topic, 0); try (var admin = Admin.create(Map.<String, Object>of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092"))) { List<String> missing = new ArrayList<>(List.of(topic, dlt)); missing.removeAll(admin.listTopics().names().get()); if (!missing.isEmpty()) admin.createTopics(missing.stream().map(t -> new NewTopic(t, 1, (short) 1)).toList()).all().get(); } var producer = new KafkaProducer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", "key.serializer", StringSerializer.class, "value.serializer", StringSerializer.class)); String[][] payments = { {"acct-1", "pay-0,authorize,1000"}, {"acct-7", "pay-1,authorize,2500"}, {"acct-3", "pay-2,authorize,4000"}, {"acct-7", "pay-3,capture,12x50"}, {"acct-1", "pay-4,capture,1000"}, {"acct-7", "pay-5,refund,1250"}, {"acct-3", "pay-6,capture,4000"}, {"acct-7", "pay-7,authorize,3000"}}; long start = -1; for (String[] p : payments) { long offset = producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(topic, 0, p[0], p[1])).get().offset(); if (start < 0) start = offset; } Map<String, Long> parked = new HashMap<>(); // key -> offset of the failed record it waits behind try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092", "group.id", "ledger-dlt-demo", "enable.auto.commit", false, "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class))) { c.assign(List.of(tp)); c.seek(tp, start); // this run's eight payments List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> records = new ArrayList<>(); while (records.size() < payments.length) records.addAll(c.poll(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).records(tp)); for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) { String at = "offset " + r.offset() + " " + r.key() + " " + r.value() + ":"; Long behind = parked.get(r.key()); if (behind != null) { deadLetter(producer, dlt, r, "parked behind offset " + behind, "sfz.ParkedKey"); System.out.println(at + " parked behind offset " + behind + " -> " + dlt); continue; } for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++) { try { handle(r); System.out.println(at + " applied" + (attempt > 1 ? " on attempt " + attempt : "")); break; } catch (IssuerTimeout e) { if (attempt == 3) { deadLetter(producer, dlt, r, e.getMessage(), e.getClass().getName()); System.out.println(at + " gave up after 3 attempts -> " + dlt); if (park) parked.put(r.key(), r.offset()); break; } long wait = 100L << (attempt - 1); // 100 ms, then 200 ms System.out.println(at + " attempt " + attempt + " failed (" + e.getMessage() + "), retry in " + wait + " ms"); Thread.sleep(wait); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { deadLetter(producer, dlt, r, e.getMessage() == null ? "" : e.getMessage(), e.getClass().getName()); System.out.println(at + " " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ", no retry -> " + dlt); if (park) parked.put(r.key(), r.offset()); break; } } } long next = records.get(records.size() - 1).offset() + 1; c.commitSync(Map.of(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(next))); // after every dead letter is acked System.out.println("committed offset " + next + ": the partition is not stuck"); } producer.close(); } static void deadLetter(KafkaProducer<String, String> p, String dlt, ConsumerRecord<String, String> r, String why, String cls) throws Exception { var record = new ProducerRecord<>(dlt, r.key(), r.value()); record.headers() .add("dlt.original.topic", r.topic().getBytes()) .add("dlt.original.partition", Integer.toString(r.partition()).getBytes()) .add("dlt.original.offset", Long.toString(r.offset()).getBytes()) .add("dlt.exception.class", cls.getBytes()) .add("dlt.exception.message", why.getBytes()); p.send(record).get(); // wait for the broker's ack before the offset may be committed } }

sections.h: Long waits belong in retry topics, not in the poll loop
sections.html:
In-place retries handle a hiccup. They can't handle an outage. Say the card issuer is down for 3 minutes. Waits of 100, 200 and 400 ms give up in under a second, and every payment of those 3 minutes lands in the DLT: 5,400 records for a person to replay. Stretch the waits to 30 seconds and up to 6 attempts instead, and one payment holds its partition for 3 minutes while 5,400 others queue behind it, with the poll loop dangerously close to max.poll.interval.ms.

The fix is to wait somewhere else. A queue broker can make one message wait while the rest flow past: since RabbitMQ 4.4 a quorum-queue message can carry a delivery time. A log can't, because its bookmark is one number per partition. So Kafka consumers build the wait out of separate topics. Retry topics form a staircase of topics with growing delays: payments.retry-10s, then payments.retry-1m, then payments.DLT. When a record still fails after its quick in-place retries, the main consumer writes it to payments.retry-10s, commits, and moves on to the next payment at full speed. The record's timestamp says when it was written, so the retry consumer knows it is due 10 seconds later.

A separate consumer group reads each retry topic. When the head of a partition isn't due yet, it doesn't sleep: it calls pause on that partition and keeps calling poll, which keeps it in the group (lesson 8) and returns nothing for paused partitions. When the record is due, it calls resume, seeks back to the record, and processes it. A failure there sends the record one step down the staircase; the last step is the DLT. Every record in one retry topic waits the same 10 seconds, so they come due in the order they were written, and the consumer only ever waits for the record at the head.

Frameworks build this staircase for you. Spring for Apache Kafka has @RetryableTopic; Quarkus has the delayed-retry-topic failure strategy. It is worth knowing what they do, because the staircase has a cost they can't hide. A record in a retry topic has left its partition, and the payments behind it in that partition carry on without it. For many records that is fine. For a payment it is a problem, and the next section deals with it.

sections.h: A payment must not overtake its own failure
sections.html:
Look at acct-7 in the Try-it. pay-1 authorizes 25.00. pay-3 captures 12.50, but its amount is broken, so it goes to the DLT. pay-5 refunds the 12.50 and is applied, a refund of a capture that never happened. Next morning someone fixes pay-3 and replays it, and the capture lands after its refund. Lesson 5 promised that one account's payments stay in order because they share a partition. The DLT broke that promise for acct-7. A retry topic breaks it the same way, only for a shorter time. On lesson 1's queue the question hardly comes up: competing consumers and redelivery reorder messages anyway. A log keeps per-key order, so it is yours to lose.

The fix is to park the key. Once a record of acct-7 has gone to the DLT or a retry topic, every later record of acct-7 follows it there, with a header naming the record it waits behind, until the first one is resolved. Other accounts keep flowing. When pay-3 is fixed, the replay tool sends acct-7's three dead letters back in their original order. In code it is one check before the handler:

Java
String blockedBy = parked.get(r.key());
if (blockedBy != null) {
    dlt.send(DeadLetters.deadLetter(r, new ParkedKeyException(blockedBy), "payments.DLT")).get();
    continue;                                  // acct-7 waits behind its failed payment
}
Kotlin
val blockedBy = parked[r.key()]
if (blockedBy != null) {
    dlt.send(DeadLetters.deadLetter(r, ParkedKeyException(blockedBy), "payments.DLT")).get()
    continue                                   // acct-7 waits behind its failed payment
}

Where does the set of parked keys live? The lab keeps it in memory, and that isn't enough in production. After a restart, or after a rebalance moves the partition to another member (lesson 8), the new consumer has an empty set, and acct-7's next payment goes straight through. Keep the set where it survives: a table in the ledger database, or a compacted topic keyed by account (lesson 3), loaded in onPartitionsAssigned.

Parking isn't always worth it. If a key's records are independent, such as notification emails or audit events, a little reordering does no harm, and you can let the rest through. Park whenever records of a key build on each other: balances, state machines like authorize, capture and refund, anything an idempotency check can't put back in order. And alert on parked accounts. Parking turns one bad record into one stuck customer, which is far better than a stuck partition but still needs a person.

refs.title: KafkaConsumer (Kafka 4.4 javadoc): pause, resume and seek

analogy: Think of a cashier's lane at a supermarket. A customer whose card is declined because the terminal lost its connection can wait a moment and try again: that is a transient failure, and a couple of retries fix it. A customer with a cart full of items that have no price can't be served by trying again. A good cashier doesn't hold the whole queue: the cart goes to the service desk with a note saying what was wrong, and the queue moves on. That desk is the dead-letter topic, and the note is the headers. The analogy breaks with families: if the same family has three carts in the queue and the first went to the desk, the other two must follow it there, or the family's purchases get rung up out of order. Real cashiers don't have to care about that. A payments consumer does.
world: In Quarkus, the SmallRye connector's failure-strategy attribute decides what happens when your @Incoming method fails: fail (the default) stops the channel, which is the poison pill; ignore commits past it and loses the payment; dead-letter-queue writes it to dead-letter-topic-<channel> with headers such as dead-letter-reason and dead-letter-offset; delayed-retry-topic builds the retry staircase. Use SmallRye Fault Tolerance's @Retry on the method for quick in-place retries, but list only transient exceptions in it. None of these park keys, so for the ledger, keep a parked-accounts table in Oracle, checked in the same transaction as the idempotency key from lesson 7, and route a parked account's payments to the DLT yourself. If a payment kicks off a Temporal workflow, Temporal's activity retry policy can take over the transient retries, and the Kafka consumer only has to start the workflow.
mistake: Logging and committing past a failure (catch (e) { log.error(...) }), or the framework equivalent of ignore. The partition never gets stuck, so it looks healthy, and every failure silently loses a payment: a missing ledger entry that someone finds weeks later during reconciliation, with the record long gone by retention. The opposite mistake is just as common: retrying everything forever, which turns one bad record into a stopped partition. The fix: classify exceptions, retry only the transient ones and only a few times, send everything else to a DLT with headers, commit only after the dead letter is acknowledged, and put an alert on the DLT.

java.title: Java
java.html: static ProducerRecord<String, String> deadLetter(ConsumerRecord<String, String> failed, Throwable error, String dlt) { var record = new ProducerRecord<>(dlt, null, failed.key(), failed.value()); // partition from the key for (Header h : failed.headers()) record.headers().add(h); // keep the producer's headers record.headers() .add("dlt.original.topic", utf8(failed.topic())) .add("dlt.original.partition", utf8(Integer.toString(failed.partition()))) .add("dlt.original.offset", utf8(Long.toString(failed.offset()))) .add("dlt.exception.class", utf8(error.getClass().getName())) .add("dlt.exception.message", utf8(error.getMessage() == null ? "" : error.getMessage())); return record; } static byte[] utf8(String s) { return s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8); }

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: fun deadLetter(failed: ConsumerRecord<String, String>, error: Throwable, dlt: String): ProducerRecord<String, String> { val record = ProducerRecord<String, String>(dlt, null, failed.key(), failed.value()) // partition from the key failed.headers().forEach { record.headers().add(it) } // keep the producer's headers record.headers() .add("dlt.original.topic", failed.topic().toByteArray()) .add("dlt.original.partition", failed.partition().toString().toByteArray()) .add("dlt.original.offset", failed.offset().toString().toByteArray()) .add("dlt.exception.class", error.javaClass.name.toByteArray()) .add("dlt.exception.message", (error.message ?: "").toByteArray()) return record }

compare.note: Header values are bytes in both languages, so every number becomes a string first. Kotlin's toByteArray() uses UTF-8 by default; Java's getBytes() without an argument uses the platform charset, so the Java version passes UTF-8 explicitly. Kotlin's ?: replaces the null check on the message: Exception() without a message gives null in both. In both, the partition is null, so the producer picks it from the key and an account's dead letters stay together and in order.

If it happened first and the DLT write then failed, // the record would be in neither place: lost. recap: A record that fails every time (a poison pill) stops its partition: the bookmark can't pass it and nothing counts the attempts. A queue broker counts deliveries and gives up; a Kafka consumer must do that itself.
Sort failures by exception type: retry transient ones a few times with exponential backoff; send permanent ones to a dead-letter topic at once.
A dead letter keeps the key and value and adds headers: original topic, partition, offset, exception. Wait for its ack, then commit.
A deserialization failure throws RecordDeserializationException from poll on every call; seek past it, after saving its bytes.
Long waits go to retry topics with fixed delays, so the main partition keeps moving. Anything that leaves the partition can be overtaken.
For payments, park the key: later records of a failed account follow it to the DLT, in order, until it is resolved.

explain.prompt: On-call got paged: one partition of payments has a lag of 40,000 and growing, while the other eleven are at 0. Explain what most likely happened, why the other partitions are fine, and what the consumer should do differently.
explain.answer: Most likely a poison pill: one record in that partition fails every time we process it, say an amount we can't parse. Our consumer lets the exception escape before the commit, so it restarts at the committed offset, reaches the same record and fails again, forever. The bookmark can't move past it, so every payment written to that partition since then is waiting. The other partitions have their own bookmarks and other members' attention, so they keep flowing. The consumer should sort failures: retry the transient ones, like issuer timeouts, a few times with backoff; send permanent ones to a dead-letter topic at once, with headers for the original topic, partition, offset and exception; wait for that write's ack and then commit. Because these are payments, it should also park the account, so the account's later payments go to the DLT behind the failed one instead of overtaking it, and keep the parked accounts in a table so a restart doesn't forget them. Then someone fixes the record and replays the account's dead letters in order, and the idempotency keys make the replay safe.

deeper.html:
Saving undeserializable records. When poll throws RecordDeserializationException, the exception holds everything you need to dead-letter the record without the deserializer: topicPartition(), offset(), timestamp(), headers(), and the raw keyBuffer() and valueBuffer(). Write those bytes to the DLT with a byte-array producer, then seek past. Another approach is to consume as byte[] and deserialize in your handler, so a bad record becomes an ordinary handler failure. Spring's ErrorHandlingDeserializer wraps a deserializer to do the same.

Retry topics without sleeping. The retry consumer's trick is pause(partitions) plus poll. A paused partition returns no records, but the loop keeps calling poll, so the member stays in the group and max.poll.interval.ms is never in danger. Store the due time in a header or compute it from the record timestamp, and resume the partition when the head record is due. Use one topic per delay: if a topic mixed 10-second and 10-minute delays, a 10-minute record at the head would hold back 10-second records behind it.

Share groups and acknowledgements. Lesson 11 covers share groups, where each record is acknowledged on its own: RELEASE returns it for another attempt, REJECT gives up on it, and the broker counts deliveries (share.delivery.count.limit, 5 by default). Kafka 4.4 added a broker-side dead-letter queue for share groups (KIP-1191). They give up per-key order across consumers, so for payments the parking problem above remains yours.
